title: Battery Engineering Notebook #010 SOC, SOH & SOP How does the BMS know the state of a battery?
excerpt: A battery has no way to report its own state directly. This notebook looks at the three estimates a BMS builds from voltage, current and temperature: state of charge, state of health and state of power, what each one means, how it is calculated, why it drifts, and how the three are connected.

children.text: In the previous notebook, we moved deeper into the electrical behavior of the lithium-ion cell. We saw that a battery is not an ideal voltage source, and that internal resistance and impedance influence voltage drop, heat generation, power capability and the way the battery responds to changing loads.
But understanding battery behavior creates another fundamental question. How do we know what state the battery is actually in?

A driver may look at an EV dashboard and see 65% battery. But what does that 65% actually mean? How does the vehicle know how much charge remains? How does it know whether the battery has degraded after years of operation? And how does it determine how much power the battery can safely deliver during acceleration or accept during regenerative braking and charging?

These questions lead us to three fundamental concepts in battery management: State of Charge, State of Health and State of Power, commonly abbreviated as SOC, SOH and SOP. Although they are often presented together, they answer three different questions about the battery.
SOC: how full is the battery?
State of charge is the charge remaining in a cell, expressed as a percentage of its usable capacity. There are two basic ways to estimate it, and each one fails in a different way.

Coulomb counting adds up the current flowing in and out of the battery over time. It responds instantly and is accurate over short periods, but small errors in the current sensor accumulate, and it needs a correct starting value.

Voltage lookup uses the fact that the open-circuit voltage (OCV) of a rested cell changes with SOC. It is accurate only when the battery has been resting, because voltage sags under load and recovers slowly afterwards. On chemistries such as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) the OCV curve is very flat through the middle of the range, so a tiny voltage error becomes a large SOC error.

Production BMS software combines the two. Coulomb counting does the moment-to-moment tracking, and a model-based observer, often a Kalman filter running on an equivalent circuit model of the cell, uses the measured voltage to keep pulling the estimate back towards reality. Many systems also recalibrate when the battery is fully charged or has rested for long enough.
SOH: how worn is the battery?
State of health describes how far a battery has aged compared with when it was new. Two definitions are in common use.
Capacity-based SOH is the present usable capacity divided by the rated capacity. It tells you how much range has been lost.
Resistance-based SOH tracks the growth of internal resistance. It tells you how much power capability has been lost.

Capacity can be estimated by comparing the charge counted between two well-known SOC points, for example during a long charge. Resistance can be estimated from how much the voltage jumps when the current changes suddenly. Ageing is driven by temperature, charge and discharge rate, depth of cycling and time spent at a high state of charge, which is why the same pack can age very differently in two vehicles. Many manufacturers treat a battery as reaching the end of its first life at somewhere around 70 to 80 percent of its original capacity, though the exact threshold depends on the warranty and the application.
SOP: how much power is available right now?

State of power is the maximum power the battery can deliver, or absorb during regenerative braking and charging, over a stated time window such as 10 or 30 seconds, without breaking any limits. Those limits are a minimum and maximum cell voltage, a maximum current and a safe temperature range.

A simplified way to see it: model the cell as a voltage source (its OCV) in series with a resistance R. For discharge, the largest current that keeps the terminal voltage above its minimum is roughly (OCV − Vmin) ÷ R, and the power is that current times the voltage. For charging, swap in the maximum voltage. Real systems add the slower polarisation effects and the temperature dependence, but the idea is the same.

This is why SOP drops when the battery is cold (resistance rises), when SOC is very low or very high (the voltage sits close to a limit), and when the battery is old (resistance has grown). It is also why an EV may limit acceleration or regenerative braking on a cold morning.
How the three estimates depend on each other

The estimates are not independent. SOC needs the present capacity, which comes from SOH, because the same amount of charge is a larger percentage of a worn battery. SOP needs SOC, temperature and resistance. An error in one estimate feeds into the others, which is why a good BMS treats them as one connected problem and keeps track of how uncertain each figure is.
Why it is hard
Current and voltage sensors have offset and gain errors, and those errors change with temperature.
Some chemistries show hysteresis, meaning the voltage at a given SOC depends on whether the cell was last charged or discharged.
Cells in a pack differ from one another, and the differences grow with age.
The parameters of the model drift as the battery ages, so the model has to be updated over time.

In short, the BMS never measures the state of a battery directly. It runs a model, compares the model with the measurements, and corrects itself continuously. The quality of the estimate depends on good sensors, a good model and an honest account of uncertainty.

title: Battery Engineering Notebook #001: Understanding the Heart of Every Electric Vehicle
excerpt: The battery isn't just a power source. It shapes an EV's cost, range, charging speed, lifespan, resale value and even its design. Here is why understanding the battery means understanding the vehicle itself.

children.text: "Before we can understand electric vehicles, we must first understand their heart."
Every conversation about electric vehicles eventually arrives at one topic: The Battery.

Some people talk about range, others focus on charging speed, fleet operators think about operating costs, engineers debate chemistry, thermal management, and battery degradation. Investors look at battery prices before evaluating the future of the EV industry while manufacturers spend billions of dollars researching new battery technologies.

Different conversations, but they all revolve around this one critical component. It is the single most expensive, influential, and arguably the most misunderstood component in an electric vehicle. Despite this, many discussions about EV batteries rarely go beyond a few familiar questions:
How long does it last?
How far can it go?
How much does it cost to replace?
While these are valid questions, they barely scratch the surface of what a modern EV battery truly is.

A battery is not simply a large box that stores electricity but rather a highly engineered electrochemical energy system consisting of hundreds, or even thousands of individual lithium-ion cells working together under the continuous supervision of sophisticated electronics known as the Battery Management System (BMS). Every second, the battery is making decisions, monitoring temperatures, balancing cells, estimating remaining energy, protecting itself from faults, and communicating with the rest of the vehicle.
In many ways, the battery is not just a component of the vehicle, it is the foundation upon which the entire vehicle is designed.
Why batteries matter more than most people realize

Imagine removing the engine from a conventional internal combustion vehicle. What remains is essentially a shell waiting for its power source. Now imagine removing the battery from an electric vehicle. The result is exactly the same.

The battery is the primary energy source that makes every other system possible. But unlike a fuel tank, which simply stores fuel, the battery actively influences almost every aspect of how an electric vehicle performs. Its influence extends far beyond supplying electrical energy. It determines how far the vehicle can travel before recharging, influences how quickly the vehicle accelerates, limits or enables fast charging, affects vehicle weight and handling, impacts safety, maintenance requirements, operating costs, resale value, and even the overall architecture of the vehicle itself.
In other words, the battery doesn't simply power the EV. It defines it.
The battery determines the cost of an electric vehicle
One of the biggest reasons electric vehicles have historically been more expensive than conventional vehicles is battery cost.

Although battery prices have fallen dramatically over the past decade thanks to advances in manufacturing, improved chemistry, and economies of scale, the battery pack still represents one of the largest cost components in an EV.
Depending on the vehicle and application, the battery can account for 30–50% of the total manufacturing cost. That single figure explains why manufacturers invest so heavily in battery research.

A small improvement in battery design can reduce production costs by millions of dollars across an entire vehicle program. This is also why companies such as Tesla, BYD, CATL, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, Samsung SDI, and others continue investing heavily in battery innovation. They understand that the future competitiveness of electric mobility will be determined as much by battery technology as by vehicle design.
The battery determines vehicle range
Ask someone why they hesitate to buy an EV, and one answer frequently appears:
"I'm worried about the range."
Range anxiety has become one of the defining conversations in electric mobility. Yet range is not determined solely by battery size, it is influenced by several engineering factors working together:
Battery capacity
Cell chemistry
Vehicle efficiency
Aerodynamics
Weight
Driving behavior
Ambient temperature
Terrain
Battery management strategies
Think of two people carrying identical water bottles. One walks calmly while the other sprints uphill. Although they started with the same amount of water, one finishes much sooner.
Similarly, two vehicles with identical battery capacities can achieve very different driving ranges depending on how efficiently they use the stored energy.
Understanding batteries therefore means understanding range.
The battery determines charging speed
One of the most common assumptions among new EV users is:
"If I install a bigger charger, my vehicle will charge faster."

In reality, charging speed is not determined by the charger alone. The battery plays the leading role. Every battery chemistry has limits on how quickly it can safely accept energy. Charge too slowly and convenience suffers. Charge too quickly and excessive heat may accelerate degradation or compromise safety. This is why manufacturers carefully balance charging performance with long-term battery health.

Behind every fast-charging session lies an intricate coordination between the charger, the vehicle, and the Battery Management System, which continuously adjusts charging current based on temperature, voltage, and the battery's state of charge.
Fast charging is therefore not simply a charger capability; it is fundamentally a battery capability.
The battery determines lifespan

Unlike a fuel tank, batteries age. Every charging cycle, every rapid acceleration, every fast-charge session, every hot afternoon, and every cold morning contributes in some way to gradual battery degradation. Fortunately, modern lithium-ion batteries are engineered to deliver many years of reliable service.

For most EV owners, battery lifespan is measured in thousands of charge cycles and often well over a decade of normal use. But longevity does not happen by chance. It results from careful engineering decisions involving:
Cell chemistry
Thermal management
Battery management algorithms
Charge and discharge limits
Cooling systems
Manufacturing quality
The battery is constantly balancing performance against longevity, and one of the greatest engineering challenges is delivering both.
The battery determines resale value
When people purchase a used internal combustion vehicle, questions often revolve around engine condition, transmission history, or mileage.

For used electric vehicles, battery condition becomes one of the most important considerations. Two identical vehicles with the same mileage may have significantly different values if one battery has experienced greater degradation. This is where concepts such as State of Health (SOH) become extremely important.

A healthy battery retains more usable capacity, offers greater driving range, supports better charging performance, and ultimately preserves vehicle value. Understanding battery health is becoming as essential in the EV industry as understanding engine condition has always been in conventional vehicles.
The battery shapes vehicle design
Perhaps one of the least appreciated facts about electric vehicles is that the battery does not simply fit into the vehicle. The vehicle is designed around the battery.
Battery dimensions influence:
Vehicle floor height
Wheelbase
Cabin space
Centre of gravity
Crash structure
Weight distribution
Suspension design
Cooling architecture

This is one reason why many modern EVs offer spacious interiors despite having similar exterior dimensions to conventional vehicles. By integrating the battery into the chassis, engineers can improve structural rigidity, lower the centre of gravity, and create entirely new design possibilities.
In many modern platforms, the battery is no longer just an energy source. It is part of the vehicle's structure.
The most misunderstood component in an EV

Despite its importance, the battery remains one of the most misunderstood engineering systems in electric mobility. Many people think of it as one large rechargeable battery. In reality, it is an ecosystem.
Inside a modern battery pack are:
Hundreds to thousands of individual cells.
Modules that organize those cells.
High-voltage contactors.
Current sensors.
Voltage sensing circuits.
Thermal management systems.
Cooling channels.
High-voltage fuses.
Pre-charge circuits.
Isolation monitoring.
Battery Management Systems running complex estimation and protection algorithms.
Every one of these systems must work together seamlessly to ensure safety, reliability, and performance. A failure in any one of them can affect the operation of the entire vehicle.
Why this series exists

The world is entering an era where batteries will shape not only transportation, but also energy storage, renewable integration, heavy industry, aviation, and marine applications. Yet much of the discussion surrounding batteries remains limited to headlines and simplified explanations.

As engineers, technicians, fleet operators, students, business leaders, and EV enthusiasts, we owe it to ourselves to understand the technology that is transforming mobility. That is the purpose of this series.

Over the coming weeks, we will progressively unpack battery engineering, from the fundamentals to advanced concepts used in modern electric vehicles. We will explore not only what batteries are, but why engineers make the design decisions they do.

Because in engineering, there is rarely a single "best" solution. There are only well-considered trade-offs. Understanding those trade-offs is what separates memorizing facts from thinking like an engineer.
Looking ahead
In the next edition of Battery Engineering Notebook, we begin with the building block of every battery: the lithium-ion cell.
We'll answer questions such as:
What actually happens inside a battery when it charges?
Why does lithium move between electrodes?
Why are there so many different battery chemistries?
Why does Tesla use one chemistry while BYD often chooses another?
Is there really such a thing as the "best" EV battery?

Those answers begin at the smallest unit of the entire battery pack: the cell. Therefore, before we can understand modules, packs, Battery Management Systems, or electric vehicles themselves we must first understand the cell.

Every electric vehicle is ultimately a story of energy: how it is stored, managed, protected, and delivered. The battery is not just another component in that story; it is the chapter from which every other chapter begins.

title: Battery Engineering Notebook #002 Everything Starts with a Single Cell
excerpt: Every battery pack, no matter the brand, is built from the same fundamental unit: the lithium-ion cell. Here is what a cell actually is, its four core components, and why understanding it is the first step to understanding any EV.

children.text: "The journey to understanding electric vehicles doesn't begin with the motor, the charger, or even the battery pack. It begins with something small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, a lithium-ion cell."

In the previous edition of Battery Engineering Notebook, we explored why the battery is the heart of every electric vehicle. We saw that it is far more than an energy source; it is the component that largely determines an EV's range, performance, charging speed, lifespan, safety, cost, and even its resale value. In many ways, understanding electric vehicles begins with understanding their batteries.
But that naturally raises another question.
What exactly is a battery?

If you were to dismantle the battery pack of a Tesla Model Y, a BYD Seal, a Nissan Leaf, or an electric bus, you would find that despite their different designs and performance characteristics, they all share the same fundamental building block: the lithium-ion cell.

Everything else, the battery modules, the cooling system, the Battery Management System (BMS), the high-voltage wiring, and the protective enclosure is built around this single electrochemical device.
Understanding the cell is therefore the first step towards understanding every electric vehicle on the road today.
Why battery engineers start with the cell

Imagine trying to understand how a city functions without first understanding a single building. Or attempting to study the human body without first learning about biological cells. The larger system only begins to make sense once its smallest functional unit is understood.
Battery engineering follows exactly the same principle.

Every battery pack, regardless of its size or application, is simply a carefully engineered collection of individual cells working together as one energy storage system. Whether the battery powers an electric motorcycle, a passenger car, a delivery van, or a heavy-duty truck, its performance ultimately depends on the behavior of thousands of individual cells.
This is why battery engineers spend so much time studying a component that most people never even see.
A battery is more than a battery
One of the most common misconceptions is referring to the entire high-voltage battery as simply "the battery."
From an engineering perspective, however, the battery is built in layers.
At the smallest level is the cell. Multiple cells are combined to form a module, and several modules are assembled into a battery pack, which is then integrated into the vehicle.

A useful analogy is constructing a building. A single brick is not a house, yet every house begins with individual bricks. Those bricks form walls, the walls form rooms, and together they become a complete structure.

Likewise, one lithium-ion cell cannot power an electric vehicle. Thousands of carefully connected cells form modules, the modules form the battery pack, and the battery pack becomes the vehicle's energy source.
Every electric vehicle, regardless of brand or size, starts with the same principle. Everything begins with a single cell.
What is a lithium-ion cell?

At first glance, a lithium-ion cell appears deceptively simple. It is often no larger than a soft drink can or a slim rectangular block. Yet inside that compact structure lies one of the most sophisticated electrochemical systems ever engineered.

Contrary to what many people assume, a battery does not store electricity in the way a water tank stores water. Instead, it stores chemical energy. Whenever you press the accelerator, a carefully controlled electrochemical reaction converts that stored chemical energy into electrical energy, which then powers the electric motor.
When you plug the vehicle into a charger, the process reverses. Electrical energy from the grid is converted back into chemical energy and stored inside the battery, ready for the next journey.
Every trip an EV makes is therefore powered by a continuous conversion between chemistry and electricity.
The world's smallest power plant
Perhaps the best way to visualize a lithium-ion cell is to imagine it as a miniature energy factory.

Like any factory, it has raw materials, transport systems, storage areas, and processes that transform one form of energy into another. Instead of workers moving products along conveyor belts, billions of lithium ions shuttle between two electrodes. Instead of producing manufactured goods, the cell produces electrical energy capable of moving an entire vehicle.

This movement is invisible to the driver, yet it is happening every second the vehicle accelerates, climbs a hill, recovers energy during regenerative braking, or charges at a station. Behind every smooth and silent EV journey is an extraordinary amount of electrochemical activity.
The four components that make every lithium-ion cell work
Although different manufacturers use different battery chemistries, almost every lithium-ion cell contains four essential components that work together to store and release energy.
The anode, commonly made from graphite, serves as the host for lithium ions during charging. It acts much like a warehouse, storing lithium until the energy is needed.

The cathode is equally important because it largely determines the battery's characteristics. Factors such as energy density, lifespan, charging speed, thermal stability, safety, and cost are heavily influenced by the cathode material. In fact, when engineers refer to chemistries such as LFP, NMC, or NCA, they are primarily referring to different cathode compositions.

Connecting these two electrodes is the electrolyte, a specially formulated medium that allows lithium ions to move between them. An important point often overlooked is that electrons do not travel through the electrolyte. Only lithium ions move inside the battery. The electrons follow an entirely different path through the external electrical circuit, creating the electric current that powers the motor.

Separating the two electrodes is the separator, a remarkably thin but critically important component. It physically prevents the anode and cathode from touching, which would create an internal short circuit, while still allowing lithium ions to pass through its microscopic pores. Despite rarely receiving attention, the separator is one of the battery's most important safety features.
Together, these four components form the foundation of every lithium-ion battery used in modern electric vehicles.
Where does the electricity actually come from?
One of the biggest misconceptions about batteries is the idea that electricity somehow sits inside them waiting to be released.

That is not what happens. The electricity produced by a battery is a direct consequence of electrochemical reactions occurring inside the cell. As lithium ions move internally between the electrodes, electrons are forced to travel through the external circuit because they cannot pass through the electrolyte.
Those moving electrons constitute the electric current that powers the vehicle.
No electrochemical reaction means no movement of lithium ions.
No movement of lithium ions means no flow of electrons.
No flow of electrons means no electricity.
And without electricity, the motor cannot produce motion.
In other words, every journey begins with the movement of lithium.
Why is it called a lithium-ion battery?

The answer lies in the name itself. Notice that we call it a lithium-ion battery, not a lithium-electron battery. Lithium ions are the active species responsible for storing and releasing energy. During charging, they move from the cathode to the anode, where they are stored. During discharge, they travel back to the cathode while electrons flow through the external circuit, powering the motor.

Unlike petrol in an internal combustion engine, lithium is not consumed during this process. Instead, it continuously shuttles back and forth between the two electrodes, repeating the same journey thousands of times throughout the battery's life.
The efficiency and stability of this movement ultimately determine how well the battery performs over many years of service.
An intelligent system, even at rest
Many people assume that once an electric vehicle is parked, the battery becomes inactive.

In reality, the battery never truly sleeps. Even while the vehicle is stationary, the Battery Management System continuously monitors cell voltages, temperatures, current flow, State of Charge (SOC), State of Health (SOH), insulation status, and numerous other parameters that ensure safe operation.

Modern EV batteries are no longer passive energy storage devices. They are intelligent systems, constantly monitoring themselves to maximize performance, protect against failure, and extend battery life.
The beginning of engineering trade-offs
By now, another important question naturally emerges.
If every electric vehicle starts with a lithium-ion cell, why don't all manufacturers simply build the same battery?

The answer introduces one of the most fundamental principles in engineering. There is rarely a perfect solution, only trade-offs. Some batteries store more energy but charge more slowly. Others prioritize safety over energy density. Some deliver exceptional power, while others are designed to maximize lifespan or minimize cost.

Every battery chemistry represents a different balance between competing objectives. This explains why companies such as Tesla, BYD, BMW, Hyundai, Mercedes-Benz, CATL, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, and others make different engineering decisions. They are not necessarily pursuing the same goal. Each is optimizing its battery for a particular vehicle, customer, operating environment, and business strategy.
The question, therefore, is not "Which battery is the best?" The better question is: "Which battery is best for this application?" That distinction lies at the heart of battery engineering.
Looking ahead

We've now identified the fundamental building block of every EV battery and explored the key components that make a lithium-ion cell possible. But we still haven't answered perhaps the most fascinating question of all.
How does this small collection of graphite, metal oxides, electrolyte, and separator actually generate electricity?

Why do lithium ions move from one electrode to another? What causes electrons to flow through the external circuit? And what exactly happens inside the cell every time we charge or drive an electric vehicle?
Those questions take us into the elegant world of electrochemistry, where oxidation, reduction, voltage, and lithium-ion movement come together to transform stored chemical energy into motion.
And that's where we'll continue in Battery Engineering Notebook #3.
